newsitem.title: FRANCE: French privatisation debacles -the job gets harder.
newsitem.headline: French privatisation debacles -the job gets harder.

text.p: The French government's decisions to break off the sale of state electronics company Thomson and CIC bank may be just the tip of the iceberg for privatisation woes.

The government already had a tough job on its hands with future privatisations of insurer GAN, Air France and troubled bank Credit Lyonnais. Only the planned partial sale of France Telecom is an exception.

The two latest U-turns make matters worse to the extent that they smack of government mismanagement and show just how easily an already difficult job can go badly awry in the face of political, trade union and staff resistance.

The sale of defence and consumer electronics giant Thomson to Lagardere was suspended on Wednesday because of privatisation commission objections to the planned onward sale of the Thomson Multimedia (TMM) consumer electronics arm to Daewoo Electronics of South Korea.
The tender for the sale of Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC) was called off on November 14 after attracting only one eligible bidder from two candidates, both French banks.

In both cases, the government opted for a process of direct sale by tender, with strict conditions for potential buyers in the case of CIC and a procedure widely criticised for its lack of transparency in the case of the Thomson.

For France Telecom, the sale of an expected 20 percent next year promises to be easier because telecoms shares are highly prized by investors, as shown by the recent scramble for Deutsche Telekom shares, and the procedure will be a more transparent competititive share issue.
The Thomson case was by nature more tricky, not only because the company is loss-making, but also because of the strategic concerns of privatising a firm involved in defence.
But it looks to have been seriously mishandled.

There was hardly any explanation from the government when it said it preferred an offer from Lagardere to a rival bid from Alcatel and that it would recapitalise Thomson SA to the tune of 11 billion francs ($2.09 billion) before selling it for a symbolic one franc.
Then Prime Minister Alain Juppe enraged staff, already up in arms about their future in South Korean hands, when he said TMM, the world's second largest television maker, was worth nothing.

In the case of CIC, the government insisted that any buyers would have to respect the integrity of the regional bank grouping and commercial ties with its parent company, the state insurer Groupe des Assurances Nationales (GAN).
It has now fired GAN chairman Jean-Jacques Bonnaud on the grounds that he did not promote the sell-off.
Bonnaud had reservations about selling CIC before going ahead with the planned sale of GAN itself and, again, the strategy chosen by the government failed to lure many suitors.
Now the government has an even tougher task on its hands.
It has vowed to privatise CIC and Thomson despite the latest debacles.

It also wants to sell GAN, but has already put unions on a war-footing in its handling of the CIC sale and will have to inject huge funds to attract investors to a group that got badly burned from investment in property before the bottom fell out of the market.

Credit Lyonnais's woes are legend. What was once the world's largest bank outside Japan suddenly announced losses of 21 billion francs in 1992-1994 as it began to pay for runaway expansion and it now lurches from one rescue package to another.

Although Air France hopes to return to profitability soon, staff are already unhappy with current restructuring plans and the privatisation of a national carrier also risks opposition from unions strongly attached to the idea of a public service and distrusting of European deregulation. ($1=5.271 French Franc)
